primary_topics: Address at the 4th Integrity Summit sponsored by the Makati Business Club and the European Chamber of Commerce, September 19, 2014 -- on judicial reform, anti-corruption, and the judiciary's role in nurturing prosperity

CJP's full judicial philosophy and reform program: APJR (Davide's model continued by CJP); ACID problems (Access, Corruption, Incompetence, Delay); four Ins (Integrity, Independence, Industry, Intelligence); plague of ships; DHL (Dedication, Honesty, Loyalty); Global Forum on Liberty and Prosperity (October 2006); Manila Declaration; FLP as the retirement-era continuation

Constitutional interpretation debate: textualists/originalists (Scalia) vs. living Constitution/social engineers (CJP/Kennedy) -- with the Tanada v. Angara WTO case as CJP's definitive statement of deferential interpretation on economic matters and strict scrutiny on civil liberties

Key SC decisions analyzed: Tanada v. Angara (WTO upheld; deferential interpretation); Manila Prince v. GSIS (Manila Hotel; CJP dissented); Belgica v. Exec. Sec. (PDAF struck down; reversal of LAMP); Gamboa v. Teves (40% foreign ownership; Carpio; prospective application urged); MOA-AD (TRO issued; FAB no TRO -- transparency made the difference)
sub_topics: Two corruption jokes as openers: (1) judge returns P50,000 to 'level the playing field' after receiving P250,000 and P200,000 from opposing counsels; (2) judge buys two P1,000 Mercedes Benz cars from a lawyer 'not speaking about his case' -- both illustrating the 'devilish games and witchcraft' that impelled the Integrity Initiative
No bribe-takers without bribe-givers: 'judges will not be bribed unless clients inveigle their lawyers to go beyond the outer limits of advocacy'

APJR: started by CJ Davide in 1998; supported by World Bank, UNDP, ADB, USAID, Canada, Japan, Australia, Britain, Netherlands; uploaded by World Bank as a model for all developing countries; CJP continued it with ACID focus; successors did not continue it -- World Bank deleted it from its website

CJP's Vision and Mission: four Ins (Integrity, Independence, Industry, Intelligence); resist influence, interference, indifference, insolence; impervious to plague of ships (kinship, relationship, friendship, fellowship); ACID problems; DHL (Dedication, Honesty, Loyalty) for 26,000 employees nationwide

Global Forum on Liberty and Prosperity (October 18-20, 2006): 300+ jurists from all over the world; led by CJs of Canada, Russia, France and others; Manila Declaration signed urging Philippines to lead rotating global forum; Canadian CJ Beverly McLachlin suggested adding 'Under the Rule of Law' to CJP's philosophy

Post-retirement: FLP organized using retirement pay; 10 professorial chairs in 9 law schools + Philippine Judicial Academy; with Metro Pacific Investment Corporation and Metrobank Foundation; CJ Sereno keynoted the September 18, 2012 launching; CJP urges the Integrity Initiative to assist SC in crafting its full reform program

Constitutional history: 1987 Constitution drafted by those who experienced martial law repressions; gave judiciary over-arching powers to strike down 'grave abuse of discretion... on the part of any branch or instrumentality of the Government'; not defined in Charter -- SC has wide latitude; 'our Court is the most powerful tribunal in the world'

1987 Constitution's economic nationalism + WTO's arrival in 1995: nationalistic fervor of Filipino First vs. liberalization, globalization, deregulation, privatization; Manila Prince v. GSIS (Manila Hotel case; CJP dissented -- government cannot favor a losing Filipino bidder over a winning foreign one in perpetuity)

Tanada v. Angara (May 2, 1997): CJP's ponencia upholding WTO; strict scrutiny for civil liberties; deferential interpretation for economic matters; 'responsibility for promoting... the country's economy rests primarily on its political leaders... people can replace them during periodic elections'; private enterprise as engine; government ensures fair distribution and enlarges the economic pie

Recent SC decisions: Belgica v. Exec. Sec. (Nov 10, 2013) struck down PDAF unanimously -- reversing LAMP v. Sec. of Budget (Apr 24, 2012) which upheld it; also struck down some DAP acts but not DAP itself; MOA-AD got TRO (sprung on people, no transparency); FAB got no TRO (Aquino administration was transparent)
EDCA: no TRO issued despite constitutional provision on foreign military bases requiring Senate treaty -- SC calibrated its awesome powers

Gamboa v. Teves (June 28, 2011 per Carpio): 40% constitutional foreign ownership limit in public utilities computed only on voting shares, not total capital; CJP disagrees; urges prospective application to protect foreign investors who relied on DOJ/SEC interpretation

Textualist (Scalia) vs. living Constitution (CJP/Kennedy): CJP visited Scalia to invite him to the Global Forum; Scalia said 'I do not believe in international law... please see my friend Justice Anthony Kennedy'; Kennedy agreed to speak via teleconference

Closing call: support SC reform initiatives; help FLP 'reshape the mind-set of our judiciary and the legal profession not only to safeguard the liberty of our people but also to help conquer poverty and share prosperity'

stances.claim: In litigations involving civil liberties, the scales of justice should weigh heavily against the government (strict scrutiny). But in matters affecting the economy and prosperity, courts must defer to the Executive and Legislative branches (deferential interpretation) -- unless there is grave abuse of discretion. This dual standard, first articulated in Tanada v. Angara and consistently applied, is CJP's core judicial philosophy.
stances.rhetorical_move: strict-scrutiny-vs-deferential-interpretation as the master judicial framework: civil liberties = strict scrutiny; economic matters = deference to elected branches
stances.confidence: asserted as the governing principle definitively established in Tanada

stances.claim: The SC under the 1987 Constitution is 'the most powerful tribunal in the world' -- granted not just the power but the duty to strike down grave abuse of discretion 'on the part of any branch or instrumentality of the Government,' a power not even given to the US Supreme Court. Its power is 'limited only by the wisdom and self-restraint of the justices themselves.'
stances.rhetorical_move: most-powerful-tribunal argument: the 1987 Constitution's grave-abuse-of-discretion clause as the unique constitutional grant that elevates Philippine judicial power above any comparable court
stances.confidence: asserted as a comparative constitutional analysis

stances.claim: Gamboa v. Teves should have been applied prospectively -- foreign investors who relied on the DOJ/SEC interpretation that the 40% limit covers total capital (not just voting shares) should be given time to divest or adjust. Retroactive application punishes those who acted in good faith on the government's own representations.
stances.rhetorical_move: prospective-application-as-fairness argument: the principle that new constitutional interpretations should not penalize good-faith reliance on prior government representations
stances.confidence: asserted as CJP's position though not a formal opinion

notable_anecdotes: The two corruption jokes: (1) a judge who returns P50,000 to 'level the playing field' after receiving unequal bribes from both sides -- the wrong way to achieve equality; (2) a judge who buys two P1,000 Mercedes Benz cars from a lawyer who 'didn't come to talk about his pending case, just to sell cars' -- the wrong way to legalize a bribe. Both illustrate the devilish games that make the Integrity Initiative necessary.

Justice Scalia declining the Global Forum: CJP personally visited Scalia to invite him to speak. Scalia: 'You do not really want me there. I would be useless in the Forum because I do not believe in international law. When I joined the US Supreme Court, I swore to defend the US Constitution and nothing else... Please see my friend, Justice Anthony Kennedy.' Kennedy agreed to speak via teleconference.

Canadian CJ Beverly McLachlin's suggestion: at the Global Forum, McLachlin suggested CJP add 'Under the Rule of Law' to his philosophy of 'Liberty and Prosperity' -- 'a suggestion I happily accepted.'

The APJR reversal: the World Bank uploaded the APJR as a model for all developing countries; CJP's successors did not continue it; the international aid agencies discontinued assistance; 'the World Bank deleted the APJR from its website.' -- the most poignant institutional reversal noted in the corpus.

MOA-AD vs. FAB: same substantive provisions, different treatment. MOA-AD got a TRO because it was 'sprung on our people, without any transparency.' FAB got no TRO because 'the Aquino administration was transparent in its peace process.' Transparency = judicial deference.

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered September 19, 2014 at the 4th Integrity Summit at the Dusit Thane Hotel -- sponsored by the Makati Business Club and the European Chamber of Commerce -- this address by CJP opens with two corruption jokes (the judge who returns P50,000 to 'level the playing field' after receiving unequal bribes; the judge who buys two P1,000 Mercedes Benz cars from a 'car salesman' lawyer) and the principle that 'there are no bribe-takers when there are no bribe-givers.' He then presents his full judicial reform vocabulary: the APJR (Davide's 1998 program continued by CJP with ACID focus; uploaded by the World Bank as a model; later deleted when successors discontinued it), the ACID problems (Access, Corruption, Incompetence, Delay), the four Ins (Integrity, Independence, Industry, Intelligence), the plague of ships (kinship, relationship, friendship, fellowship), and DHL (Dedication, Honesty, Loyalty for 26,000 judiciary employees). He describes the October 2006 Global Forum on Liberty and Prosperity (300+ jurists from all over the world; Manila Declaration; Canadian CJ Beverly McLachlin's suggestion to add 'Under the Rule of Law' -- 'a suggestion I happily accepted') and FLP (organized using retirement pay, 10 professorial chairs; CJ Sereno keynoted the September 2012 launch). The constitutional analysis: the 1987 Constitution gave the SC the duty to strike down 'grave abuse of discretion on the part of any branch or instrumentality of the Government' -- 'our Court is the most powerful tribunal in the world.' His dual standard from Tanada v. Angara (May 2, 1997): strict scrutiny for civil liberties; deferential interpretation for economic matters; private enterprise as the engine; the economic pie must be enlarged and fairly divided. He analyzes recent SC decisions: Belgica reversed LAMP on PDAF; MOA-AD got a TRO (no transparency) but FAB did not (transparent process); EDCA unchallenged; Gamboa v. Teves should be applied prospectively. The constitutional interpretation debate: he personally visited Justice Scalia to invite him to the Global Forum; Scalia declined ('I do not believe in international law'); Justice Kennedy agreed to speak via teleconference. CJP belongs to the living-Constitution school: 'jurists are not mere social technicians and legal automatons; they are social engineers who courageously fix their gaze on the underlying principles and overarching aspirations of the Constitution.'
